steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on why neural networks lose plasticity during training on nonstationary problems. It should motivate the problem, explain the gap in current understanding and mitigations, describe our empirical analysis and findings, and introduce our combined 'Swiss cheese' mitigation approach.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Nonstationarity in learning and why networks must stay adaptable
- Plasticity loss: prior observations and the lack of understanding
- Our analysis: three questions and what we find
- Swiss cheese model of mitigation and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Nonstationarity
  - single task training is easy: off-the-shelf architecture + optimizer, minimal tuning -> reasonably accurate
  - but learned statistical relationships are dynamic: consumer preferences change, internet info goes out of date, words enter/leave common usage
  - RL: improving the policy changes the distribution of collected data
  - without updating predictions -> performance declines
  - common fix: reset parameters, retrain from scratch on updated data -> computational overhead, prohibitive for large models
  - goal: keep network's ability to adapt throughout training, no resets
- Plasticity loss
  - reduced ability to adapt to new tasks after training, observed independently several times: RL and supervised learning
  - prevalent, but why it occurs is vague
  - prior work: negative results, can't attribute all cases to one quantity (parameter norm, dead units)
  - mitigations: target single pathology (risk: other mechanisms) or regularize abstract properties towards init (risk: interfere with primary objective)
  - need: model combining both -> principled strategies targeting several mechanisms together
- Our analysis
  - three questions: what nonstationarity induces plasticity loss; what structural changes in parameters/features; what properties shared by networks that lost plasticity
  - multiple mechanisms unified by preactivation distribution shift
  - similar degeneracies in empirical neural tangent kernel (predictive of training pathologies)
  - known: dead units; new: unit linearization
  - target magnitude in regression explains significant fraction of earlier plasticity loss examples in deep RL
  - not exhaustive list; but several independent mechanisms (fixing one still allows loss via another)
- Swiss cheese model
  - interventions for preactivation distribution shift, regression target magnitude, parameter growth: study independently, combine for additive benefit
  - prior work: no single mechanism fully explains plasticity loss
  - combined: negligible plasticity loss in synthetic benchmarks; improves deep RL benchmarks + natural distribution shift datasets
  - best intervention per mechanism, then combine -> less combinatorial search; implications for stabilizing optimization in nonstationary problems

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Training a neural network on a single task is fairly straightforward: for popular data modalities you can usually take an off-the-shelf architecture and optimization algorithm and get a reasonably accurate model with minimal hyperparameter tuning. But the statistical relationships that machine learning systems learn are often dynamic. Consumer preferences change over time, information on the internet goes out of date, and words enter and leave common usage. In reinforcement learning systems, just improving the learner's policy changes the distribution of the data it collects for further training. If a learning system can't update its predictions in response to these changes, its performance will inevitably decline. In practice these declines in performance are often resolved by resetting the model parameters and training from scratch on updated training data, but this adds computational overhead, which can be prohibitively expensive for large models. So it is desirable to avoid needing parameter resets by keeping the network's ability to adapt to new learning signals during the whole course of training.

It has been observed independently several times that training a neural network on some learning problems reduces its ability to adapt to new tasks, both in reinforcement learning and in supervised learning. We will call this phenomenon plasticity loss in this paper. It is quite prevalent, but our understanding of why it happens is still vague. Prior work shows a number of negative results that indicate we cannot attribute all instances of plasticity loss to a single measured quantity like parameter norm or number of dead units. Because of this, methods that try to preserve plasticity usually either target a single pathology, which risks allowing plasticity loss to happen through other mechanisms that are not addressed, or regularize more abstract properties of the network towards their initial value, which risks interfering with the primary objective. A useful model of plasticity loss should combine the best of both approaches, so that we can develop principled mitigation strategies that target several independent mechanisms together.

- Our analysis
  - three questions: what nonstationarity induces plasticity loss; what structural changes in parameters/features; what properties shared by networks that lost plasticity
  - multiple mechanisms unified by preactivation distribution shift
  - similar degeneracies in empirical neural tangent kernel (predictive of training pathologies)
  - known: dead units; new: unit linearization
  - target magnitude in regression explains significant fraction of earlier plasticity loss examples in deep RL
  - not exhaustive list; but several independent mechanisms (fixing one still allows loss via another)
- Swiss cheese model
  - interventions for preactivation distribution shift, regression target magnitude, parameter growth: study independently, combine for additive benefit
  - prior work: no single mechanism fully explains plasticity loss
  - combined: negligible plasticity loss in synthetic benchmarks; improves deep RL benchmarks + natural distribution shift datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Training a neural network on a single task is fairly straightforward: for popular data modalities you can usually take an off-the-shelf architecture and optimization algorithm and get a reasonably accurate model with minimal hyperparameter tuning. But the statistical relationships that machine learning systems learn are often dynamic. Consumer preferences change over time, information on the internet goes out of date, and words enter and leave common usage. In reinforcement learning systems, just improving the learner's policy changes the distribution of the data it collects for further training. If a learning system can't update its predictions in response to these changes, its performance will inevitably decline. In practice these declines in performance are often resolved by resetting the model parameters and training from scratch on updated training data, but this adds computational overhead, which can be prohibitively expensive for large models. So it is desirable to avoid needing parameter resets by keeping the network's ability to adapt to new learning signals during the whole course of training.

It has been observed independently several times that training a neural network on some learning problems reduces its ability to adapt to new tasks, both in reinforcement learning and in supervised learning. We will call this phenomenon plasticity loss in this paper. It is quite prevalent, but our understanding of why it happens is still vague. Prior work shows a number of negative results that indicate we cannot attribute all instances of plasticity loss to a single measured quantity like parameter norm or number of dead units. Because of this, methods that try to preserve plasticity usually either target a single pathology, which risks allowing plasticity loss to happen through other mechanisms that are not addressed, or regularize more abstract properties of the network towards their initial value, which risks interfering with the primary objective. A useful model of plasticity loss should combine the best of both approaches, so that we can develop principled mitigation strategies that target several independent mechanisms together.

This paper tries to develop such a model and use it to guide the development of more effective methods to maintain plasticity. We start with an empirical analysis of three questions. First, what types of nonstationarity induce plasticity loss? Second, what types of structural changes happen to the parameters and features of neural networks when they lose plasticity? Third, what properties do networks that have lost plasticity have in common? Our analysis gives surprising answers to these questions. We find that multiple distinct mechanisms of plasticity loss can be unified by an underlying phenomenon of preactivation distribution shift, and that they result in similar degeneracies in the network's empirical neural tangent kernel (which are predictive of training pathologies). Some of the mechanisms we identify are already known, like dead units, but we also identify some surprising new ones, like unit linearization. We also find that the magnitude of the targets in regression tasks is important, and that target magnitude alone can explain a significant fraction of previous examples of plasticity loss in deep reinforcement learning. We do not try to give an exhaustive list of all the network pathologies that can lead to loss of trainability, but we show that plasticity loss can actually be driven by several independent mechanisms, meaning that an intervention which acts on one mechanism may still allow plasticity loss to happen through another.

We then use these insights to develop a 'Swiss cheese model' of mitigation strategies. We show that interventions which improve robustness to preactivation distribution shift, regression target magnitude, and parameter growth can be studied independently and then combined to give additive benefit. Prior work indicated that each mechanism on its own cannot fully explain plasticity loss, but we find that addressing several mechanisms together is enough to give negligible loss of plasticity in a variety of synthetic benchmarks, and these methods can also improve performance on deep reinforcement learning benchmarks and on natural distribution shift datasets. By finding the best interventions for each mechanism in isolation and then combining them, we can significantly reduce the combinatorial complexity of searching over mitigation strategies, and this has exciting implications for future work on stabilizing optimization in nonstationary learning problems.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Training a neural network on a single task is relatively straightforward: for popular data modalities it is usually possible to take an off-the-shelf architecture and optimization algorithm and, with minimal hyperparameter tuning, obtain a reasonably accurate model. Yet the statistical relationships learned by machine learning systems are often dynamic: consumer preferences change over time, information on the internet goes out of date, and words enter and leave common usage. In reinforcement learning systems, the very act of improving the learner's policy changes the distribution of data it collects for further training. Without the ability to update its predictions in response to these changes, a learning system's performance will inevitably decline. In practice, such declines are often resolved by resetting the model parameters and training from scratch on updated training data, but this introduces additional computational overhead which can be prohibitively expensive for large models. It is therefore desirable to avoid the need for parameter resets by maintaining the network's ability to adapt to new learning signals throughout training.

The observation that training a neural network on some learning problems reduces its ability to adapt to new tasks has been made independently several times, both in reinforcement learning [1,2,3,4] and in supervised learning [5,6]. While this phenomenon, which we refer to in this paper as plasticity loss, is quite prevalent, our understanding of why it occurs remains vague. [7] show a number of negative results indicating that we cannot attribute all instances of plasticity loss to a single measured quantity such as parameter norm or number of dead units. As a result, methods that aim to preserve plasticity typically either target a single pathology [8,9], which risks allowing plasticity loss to occur via other unaddressed mechanisms, or regularize more abstract properties of the network towards their initial value [4,10,11], which risks interfering with the primary objective. A useful model of plasticity loss should combine the best of both approaches, allowing for principled mitigation strategies which target several independent mechanisms in conjunction.

This paper aims to develop such a model and use it to guide the development of more effective methods to maintain plasticity. We begin with an empirical analysis exploring three questions: first, what types of nonstationarity induce plasticity loss? Second, what structural changes occur to the parameters and features of neural networks when they lose plasticity? Third, what properties are shared among networks which have lost plasticity? Our analysis reveals surprising answers, finding that multiple distinct mechanisms of plasticity loss can be unified by an underlying phenomenon of preactivation distribution shift, and that they result in similar degeneracies in the network's empirical neural tangent kernel (which are predictive of training pathologies). While some of the mechanisms we identify, such as dead units, are already known, we also identify surprising new ones, such as unit linearization. We further identify the importance of target magnitude in regression tasks, finding that it alone can explain a significant fraction of previous examples of plasticity loss in deep reinforcement learning. While we do not aim to provide an exhaustive list of network pathologies that can lead to loss of trainability, we show that plasticity loss can be driven by several independent mechanisms, in the sense that an intervention acting on one mechanism may still allow plasticity loss to occur through another.

We then use these insights to develop a 'Swiss cheese model' of mitigation strategies, and show that interventions which improve robustness to preactivation distribution shift, regression target magnitude, and parameter growth can be studied independently and then combined to give additive benefit. Whereas prior work indicated that no single mechanism on its own can fully explain plasticity loss [7], we find that addressing several mechanisms in conjunction is sufficient to yield negligible loss of plasticity in a variety of synthetic benchmarks, and that these methods also improve performance on deep reinforcement learning benchmarks and natural distribution shift datasets. By identifying the best intervention for each mechanism in isolation and then combining them, we can significantly reduce the combinatorial complexity of the search over mitigation strategies, a finding with exciting implications for future work on stabilizing optimization in nonstationary learning problems.
